To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the liver is the primary organ of drug metabolism, and phase II metabolism is the most prevalent form of hepatic drug metabolism; (ii) phase II metabolites have very poor membrane transport, and require carrier-mediated transport for hepatic excretion; (iii) phase II metabolism and transport may be altered by chemical modulators and disease states, and these effects may be pharmacodynamic or toxicological.

(1) the hepatic transporters OATP2 and OATP8 are important for biliary excretion of glucuronide conjugates, (2) OATP2 is also involved in the hepatic uptake of sulfate and glutathione-conjugated compounds, and (3) the transport of these conjugates is modulated by chemical and pharmacological agents
The liver is the main site of drug metabolism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms responsible for hepatic excretion and the pharmacological implications of the transport of conjugated metabolites of drugs and other xenobiotics.
the elucidation of hepatic transport mechanisms that are responsible for the excretory function of the liver in the body.

the elucidation of the mechanisms responsible for the hepatic excretion, and the pharmacological and toxicological implications, of the three most prevalent phase II metabolites, sulfate, glucuronides, and glutathiones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phase II metabolism and/or transport is not a "safety valve" for drug elimination, but rather an important determinant of drug disposition and pharmacological/toxicological activity.
the liver is the primary organ of drug metabolism, and the liver is the major organ responsible for drug elimination.

the hepatic transport of sulfate, glucuronic acid, and glutathio conjugates of drugs and xenobiotics is a complex, multifaceted process that involves the coordinated action of phase II metabolism and transport proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hepatic transport of phase II metabolites is an important mechanism for drug disposition and clearance from the body.
the liver is the primary drug-metabolizing organ, and is responsible for both metabolism and excretion.
hepatic transport of conjugated metabolites is an integral part of the phase II metabolic process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver is an active barrier that must be overcome in order to reach the systemic circulation and exert pharmacological or toxicological effects.
the hepatic transport of sulfate and glucuronide conjugates is highly dependent on the molecular weight and charge of the conjugate.

the hepatic transport of phase II metabolites is not as straightforward as it is for most parent compounds, and is often dependent on the chemical structure of the phase II metabolite, as well as the chemical nature of the parent drug.
